correction.textOverride: We can sometimes assume that the whole will be as good as each of its part. Suppose, for example, you’re in charge of a startup, and you know that everyone you’ve brought on board are productive and efficient. It might seem logic to assume that, as a result, the startup will be productive and efficient, too—but this isn’t necessarily true. The fallacy of composition fails to allow for how the different “parts” interacts with each other—if, for example, your efficient administrator and your highly skilled head of IT each assumes the other is in charge of collating prototype test results, then you have a problem. Equally, a unit composed of good people can still be working on a doomed project, and a project composed of good ideas may lack a stable center. When assembling a team with a common goal, always check the overall view as well as the individual involved.
